# R1 Digest — Green Luke NICNT: Introduction + Prologue

**Source:** Joel B. Green, The Gospel of Luke (NICNT 1997)
**Cache slice:** R1_intro_prologue_3522-4112.txt (raw 3522–4112)
**Evidence class default:** Green’s exposition unless marked secondary-literature survey.

## Claims

### C1 — Discourse-analysis method of the commentary
- **Locus:** slice §1 READING THE GOSPEL OF LUKE (near start)
- **Quote:** “discourse analysis”—correlating culture-critical and narratological concerns
- **Claim:** Green (own position): this commentary pursues “discourse analysis” correlating culture-critical and narratological concerns, not every method in the biblical-studies marketplace; it examines Luke’s literary art and narrative theology (theology, ethics, spirituality) so Luke can address contemporary readers without anachronistic construction.

### C2 — Luke self-categorizes as narrative, not “Gospel”
- **Locus:** §1.1 THE GOSPEL OF LUKE AS “NARRATIVE” (διήγησις)
- **Quote:** the author himself categorizes his work as a “narrative” or “orderly account” (and not as a “Gospel,” as the tradition has it)
- **Claim:** Green: per the Lukan preface (1:1–4), Luke calls his work διήγησις / orderly account, not “Gospel”; this invites a reading mode appropriate to narrative, especially one respecting “order.”

### C3 — Available first-century narrative genres
- **Locus:** §1.1
- **Quote:** Broadly speaking, the narrative choices available in Roman antiquity were historiography and biography… and novel
- **Claim:** Green: within first-century book culture, narrative options were historiography and biography (historical referents: events / people) versus novel (no necessary historical referent); genre decisions shape generative and interpretive expectations.

### C4 — Line between historical and nonhistorical narrative relativized
- **Locus:** §1.1
- **Quote:** the line separating historical narrative and nonhistorical cannot be sustained
- **Claim:** Green: for reading narrative, the historical/nonhistorical line cannot be sustained not because historiography lacks historical claims, but because narrative representation of history is always “partial” (selective and oriented to a hermeneutical vantage); historiography inevitably provides more and less than “what actually happened.” Crucial first task even for historiography/biography is to grapple with status as narrative text.

### C5 — Cadbury and consensus: Luke 1:1–4 as historiography preface
- **Locus:** §1.1 “The Genre of the Gospel of Luke”
- **Quote:** Since the seminal work on the preface of Luke by Henry J. Cadbury… a broad consensus has emerged that Luke 1:1–4 belongs squarely within the literary tradition of ancient historiography
- **Claim:** Survey (Cadbury + consensus Green reports): Cadbury’s preface work underwrote broad consensus that Luke 1:1–4 sits in Greco-Roman historiography; other shared features include genealogy (3:23–28), meal scenes, travel narratives, speeches, letters, dramatic episodes (Nazareth 4:16–30; Acts 27 shipwreck).

### C6 — Aune: Luke-Acts as “general history”
- **Locus:** §1.1 Genre
- **Quote:** Aune has sought to clarify… classifying it as a “general history”
- **Claim:** Survey (Aune via Green): Aune classifies Luke-Acts as “general history”—narration of important historical experiences of a single national group from origin to recent past; Luke’s “national consciousness” embraces origins of the people of “the Way” as a distinct sect within first-century Judaism.

### C7 — Callan: Luke as early “true account” history type
- **Locus:** §1.1 Genre
- **Quote:** Callan has also attempted… designating Luke’s work as one of the first examples of a type of history, concerned “to present a true account of something”
- **Claim:** Survey (Callan via Green): Callan qualifies Luke-Acts as among first examples of a history type concerned to present a true account, beginning in the first century B.C.E.

### C8 — Theology-vs-history objection dismissed
- **Locus:** §1.1 Genre
- **Quote:** no ancient historian was without motive, be it theological, apologetic, pedagogical, or whatever
- **Claim:** Green: the objection that Luke is “too motivated by his theological agenda” to be historian is weak; ancient historians had motives; modern dichotomy pitting history against theology grows from problematic philosophical/epistemological commitments and is being abandoned.

### C9 — Formal differences vs Greek historiographical prefaces
- **Locus:** §1.1 Genre
- **Quote:** Luke’s preface in Greek seems much too brief, consisting of only one sentence… transition… surprisingly abrupt… does not engage in explicit criticism of his predecessors… offers no general moral reflections
- **Claim:** Green reports problems for the consensus: formal differences from Greek historians—brevity (one sentence), abrupt style/transition into 1:5, no explicit criticism of predecessors, no general moral reflections common among Greek historians.

### C10 — Alexander: closest analogues in “scientific tradition”
- **Locus:** §1.1 Genre
- **Quote:** she finds the closest analogues to Luke 1:1–4 in the “scientific tradition”—that is, technical and professional writing on medicine, mathematics, engineering, and the like
- **Claim:** Survey (Loveday Alexander via Green): reassessing Greek preface-writing, Alexander finds closest syntactical analogues to Luke 1:1–4 in scientific/technical prefaces; she proposes Luke’s narrative presentation is “scientific” in the sense of passing on accumulated teaching tradition.

### C11 — Green’s critique of pure “scientific treatise” classification
- **Locus:** §1.1 Genre
- **Quote:** The affinities Alexander documents do not support very well the notion that Luke’s Gospel is a “scientific” treatise
- **Claim:** Green (own): Alexander’s formal/grammatical affinities do not make Luke a scientific treatise (substance discontinuity); nor do they simply negate Greco-Roman historiography identification. Genre was loosely defined; Luke also influenced by OT/later Jewish historiography (historical sequences shaping narrative theology); Luke intends a long narrative of many events with prototypes Herodotus and Thucydides; literary components (symposia, travel, speeches) support historiography comparison; dual openings 1:1–4 and 1:5–2:52 (birth narrative as actual narratological beginning intending the whole of Luke-Acts).

### C12 — Biography alternative and theocentric undercutting
- **Locus:** §1.1 Genre
- **Quote:** the Third Gospel is primarily focused on God and the fulfillment of God’s ancient purpose, so it can only in a secondary sense be classified as an account of the life of Jesus
- **Claim:** Green: primary dissenting classification is Greco-Roman biography; taken alone Luke’s Gospel is susceptible to bios classification, but with Acts less so. Primary focus on God and fulfillment of God’s purpose undercuts biography as primary genre, as does inability of bios to account for Luke-Acts as a whole. Luke is influenced by Greco-Roman (esp. biographical) forms without equating Luke-Acts to biography or “biographical succession narrative.”

### C13 — Historiography expectations for reading
- **Locus:** §1.1 Genre (end)
- **Quote:** we may anticipate a narrative in which recent history is given prominence, issues of both causation and teleology are accorded privilege, and determined research is placed in the service of persuasive and engaging instruction
- **Claim:** Green: identifying Luke-Acts as ancient historiography raises expectations of recent-history prominence, causation/teleology, and research serving persuasive instruction—alongside Luke’s professed intentions in 1:1–4.

### C14 — Canonical separation obscures Luke-Acts unity
- **Locus:** §1.2 THE UNITY OF LUKE-ACTS
- **Quote:** The unity of Luke-Acts—two volumes, one story—easily escapes the modern reader in large part due to the canonical placement of these two books
- **Claim:** Green: though Gospel and Acts may have been released separately, second-century placement put Luke among the fourfold Gospel and Acts between Gospels and Letters as bridge to Paul; canonical location makes Luke thought of first as “Gospel” and Acts as framework for Paul. In Luke’s day no such literary form “Gospel” existed; Luke’s predecessors are “narratives,” not Gospels; Luke did not set out to write a Gospel to which he later appended the early church—the narrative developed purposefully from Jesus’ earthly ministry to continuation through the early church.

### C15 — Common authorship and Acts as sequel
- **Locus:** §1.2
- **Quote:** most today would agree that these two books share a common author… Acts forms some sort of sequel to the Gospel of Luke
- **Claim:** Green reports consensus: prefaces Luke 1:1–4 and Acts 1:1–2 long imply relationship; common authorship widely assumed; Acts is sequel. Acts 1:1 refers to “first book” and “all that Jesus began to do and to teach”—summary of Third Gospel (words and deeds); “began” implies continuation; followers call on Jesus’ name as continuing presence for wholeness.

### C16 — Two volumes as papyrus-roll expediency and parallel architecture
- **Locus:** §1.2
- **Quote:** as a matter of physical expediency ancient authors divided their lengthy works into “books,” each of which fit on one papyrus roll
- **Claim:** Green: volume division need not mean new subject; max ~35-foot roll; Gospel ~19,400 words, Acts ~18,400—roughly equal rolls. Plan shows purposeful proportionality: both begin in Jerusalem; Gospel ends / Acts begins with commission + ascension; ~30-year span each; Jesus’ last days in Jerusalem and Paul’s arrest-to-Rome each ~25% of their books; conscious parallels between Jesus and disciples.

### C17 — Single narrative cycle: God’s purpose of salvation for all
- **Locus:** §1.2
- **Quote:** In it we see the working out of God’s purpose to bring salvation in all of its fullness to all people
- **Claim:** Green: whole Luke-Acts can be read as one simple narrative cycle (possibility → realization → result) serving a single aim—God’s purpose to bring full salvation to all people. Birth narrative anticipates aim; realization made probable through John, Jesus’ life/death/exaltation, commissioning/empowering of followers (Luke 3–Acts 1); Jesus dissolves barriers (ethnic, gender, age, rich/poor, righteous/sinner) even if he rarely engages non-Jews; Acts 2–15 realization (egalitarian community of Jews, Samaritans, Gentiles); Acts 16–28 results (Jewish antagonism, increasingly Gentile church as God’s purpose via Paul/Scriptures). Phrase “events that have been fulfilled among us” covers Jesus-story and early-church activity as one continuous story.

### C18 — Gospel incomplete without Acts for redemptive purpose
- **Locus:** §1.2 (end)
- **Quote:** Seen against this purpose, the Gospel of Luke is incomplete in itself
- **Claim:** Green: narrative unity requires that purpose/audience/needs account for Gospel and Acts. Incidents in Gospel anticipate Acts (e.g. Simeon 2:32 light to Gentiles; Gentile mission fully only in Acts under Spirit). Luke 24 closes plot aspects, but overarching redemptive purpose for all people leaves Gospel incomplete without Acts.

### C19 — Order as primary control of meaning; no isolated pericopes
- **Locus:** §1.3 METHOD IN READING THE GOSPEL OF LUKE
- **Quote:** the order of the narrative, Luke’s staging of events in their narrative sequence, is a primary control on the determination of meaning
- **Claim:** Green: as historiographical narrative, each event-account’s significance is incomplete alone; must be read by narrative location. Isolated pericope treatment (popular reading, lectionary preaching, tradition-critical scholarship) will not do. Narratology (order, perspective, characterization, setting, theme) is immediately relevant.

### C20 — Luke as cultural product with alternative worldview invitation
- **Locus:** §1.3
- **Quote:** the Lukan narrative is an invitation to embrace an alternative worldview and to live as if the reign of God had already revolutionized this age
- **Claim:** Green: Third Gospel is a “cultural product” (cannot be dislodged from its world without incomprehensibility) yet expresses a vision not simply equatable with reconstructed first-century context (miraculous conceptions, angels, diabolic forces; events woven with interpretation as divine-purpose fulfillment). Eschatological vision (e.g. 1:52 powerful brought down / lowly lifted) invites alternative worldview and living as if God’s reign already revolutionized the age.

### C21 — Social setting between closed narrative world and naive historicism
- **Locus:** §1.3
- **Quote:** We mean more than the world available to us only through the narrative viewed as a closed system, but less than the world often represented to us by historical-critical inquiry
- **Claim:** Green: “social setting” means more than narrative-criticism’s closed “narrative world” and less than straightforward reading of real social world into the text; Luke does not represent the real world so straightforwardly—he seeks alternative view and chooses what to emphasize/downplay. Method needs narratology plus historicism rooted in social-scientific/culture-critical sensitivities, concerned not with “History with a capital H” but (1) how Luke “ordered” (1:3) events for a teleology and (2) how model readers would hear and be shaped by episodes and whole narrative.

### C22 — Key terms: co-text, intertext, context
- **Locus:** §1.3 “Some Key Terms”
- **Quote:** Co-text refers to the string of linguistic data within which a text is set… Intertext refers to the location of a text within the larger linguistic frame… Context, finally, refers to the socio-historical realities
- **Claim:** Green defines: (1) Co-text = linguistic surroundings (sentence/paragraph/pericope/whole narrative); local co-text often paramount due to memory; co-text includes later material (promises/fulfillment; narrative needs reshaped). (2) Intertext = larger linguistic frame, especially how Luke draws on LXX; explicit citations (e.g. 3:3–6), type-scenes (e.g. birth announcement), allusions/echoes; guided by criteria of “availability” and “volume”; interest in Abraham, Moses hues, Elijah/Elisha; “echo chamber” not exclusive source-certification. (3) Context = socio-historical realities of Palestine early 1st c. C.E. and wider Greco-Roman world of latter decades; cultural scripts Luke affirms or undermines.

### C23 — Commentary prioritizes narrative significance over verification
- **Locus:** §1.3 “Narrative, History, and Historicity”
- **Quote:** Our reading of the Third Gospel is concerned above all with the “narrative” side of this equation
- **Claim:** Green: ancient historiography marked by paradox of veracity vs narrative (meaningful sequence, causation, teleology)—true of Luke as of Thucydides. This commentary focuses on sequencing and interpretive aim, not primarily sources, tradition-history transformation, or whether each episode “actually happened.” Luke’s major challenge not verifying events for readers formed by 19th-c. historicism, nor redaction-critical comparison of Mark copies (illiteracy/publishing make “readers”/“copies” anachronistic).

### C24 — Jesus-as-healer historicity illustration; veracity not Luke’s issue
- **Locus:** §1.3 Jesus-healer illustration
- **Quote:** the veracity of Jesus’ healing ministry is neither for Luke, nor apparently for his contemporaries, the point at issue
- **Claim:** Green argues (with historical-Jesus criteria of dissimilarity, multiple attestation, path to death) that the healer portrait is generally historically strong, yet Luke and contemporaries assume Jesus was a healer and contest *source/interpretation* (Beelzebul; false prophet; magician/quack in Celsus, Justin, talmudic texts; Josephus “parabolic works”). Luke wraps healing in OT cloth and Spirit-anointed domain-of-God narrative; with rare exceptions Luke’s compulsion is signification, not demonstration of veracity.

### C25 — Three programmatic statements on historicity and authority
- **Locus:** §1.3 end of historicity section
- **Quote:** Luke’s contribution does not consist in such critical chronicle-keeping… with interpretive persuasion—that is, not with validation of events but with their signification
- **Claim:** Green’s three programmatic points: (1) commentary does not answer all possible questions; window-into-redaction history already well served elsewhere. (2) Approach blurs world of/behind text by treating narrative as historical object Luke invites; Luke not uninterested in actual events but narrative is not product of that interest narrowly defined (often no dispassionate witnesses for key events). (3) Authority as Scripture rests not on claim to historical veracity but capacity to speak for God / make transparent significance; biblical narrators make no prophetic-inspiration claims; paradoxically absent narrator claims divine perspective. History as bare facts may be necessary ground for faith but not sufficient.

### C26 — Authorship identity unimportant for interpretation
- **Locus:** §1.4 WHAT OF THE QUESTION OF AUTHORSHIP?
- **Quote:** our ability or inability to identify the author of the Third Gospel is unimportant to its interpretation
- **Claim:** Green: most likely candidate is Luke the physician and sometime companion of Paul, but author did not put name in Gospel; title “according to Luke” added decades later. Identity not critical to reading (e.g. do not use physician vocation to explain healing interest). Because anonymous and little known of Paul’s Lukas (Phlm 24; Col 4:14; 2 Tim 4:11), data mostly yield “implied author”/narrator; “Luke” in commentary ≈ narrator.

### C27 — Purpose of Luke-Acts: ecclesiological strengthening
- **Locus:** §2 THE PURPOSE AND THEOLOGY OF THE GOSPEL OF LUKE
- **Quote:** the purpose of Luke-Acts would have been to strengthen the Christian movement in the face of opposition by (1) ensuring them in their interpretation and experience of the redemptive purpose and faithfulness of God and by (2) calling them to continued faithfulness and witness in God’s salvific project
- **Claim:** Green: genre suggests legitimation/apologetic; narrative unity centers God’s purpose of salvation for all. In conflicted first-century (esp. Jewish) world, purpose is primarily *ecclesiological*—practices defining/legitimating community of God’s people; invitation to participate in God’s project.

### C28 — Salvation as primary theme; theocentric narrative
- **Locus:** §2 Purpose and theology
- **Quote:** Recent scholarship has repeatedly identified “salvation” as the primary theme of Luke-Acts… Luke’s narrative is theological in substance and focus; that is, it is centered on God
- **Claim:** Green: scholarship identifies “salvation” as unifying theme; Luke is theocentric—design guiding narrative is God’s, though God rarely appears as character. Early address “God my Savior” (1:47); central journey section reconstructs followers’ view of God as Father of gracious beneficence (11:1–13; 12:32). Divine purpose surfaces directly (e.g. baptism 3:21–22) more typically via Scriptures, heavenly messengers, constellation of design terms (“purpose,” “it is necessary,” “to determine”), divine choreography; Holy Spirit is power putting God’s will into effect.

### C29 — Hermeneutical struggle over God’s purpose and Scripture
- **Locus:** §2
- **Quote:** Jesus’ struggle with the Jewish leadership and with Jewish institutions is essentially hermeneutical: Who understands God’s purpose? Who interprets the Scriptures faithfully?
- **Claim:** Green: divine-purpose emphasis serves ecclesiological/hermeneutical interests for identity over against Scripture-readers who refuse faith in Christ; coherence of God’s ancient agenda with Jesus’ ministry is crucial. Answer: Jesus’ advent rooted in ancient covenant; mission congruent with God’s intent—shown by scriptural life-pattern and resurrection/ascension vindication.

### C30 — Jesus: prophet, Davidic Messiah, Son of God, Savior
- **Locus:** §2
- **Quote:** Jesus is portrayed as a prophet, but as more than a prophet; he is the long-awaited Davidic Messiah, Son of God… Early on, Jesus is identified as Savior (2:11)
- **Claim:** Green: main character of volume one is Jesus; audience privileged early to perceive identity/role. Regal prophet for whom death is necessary but not last word; disciples struggle less with who Jesus is than how he fulfills role (conventional worldviews impede correlating exalted Messiah with suffering). Savior via healing miracles and expansive table fellowship—embodying inbreaking kingdom; “good news to the poor” (4:18–19); teaching orients to reconstructed vision of God/world order, not mere “proper behavior.”

### C31 — Discipleship, children of Abraham, Money as rival
- **Locus:** §2
- **Quote:** Genuine “children of Abraham” are those who embody in their lives the beneficence of God… chief competitor for this focus stems from Money
- **Claim:** Green: discipleship = align with Jesus and thus God; membership focuses not inherited status but behaviors of unmitigated embrace of gracious God. Practices: love enemies, do good to haters, hospitality without reciprocation, give without return—possible only after transformative encounter with God’s goodness. Chief competitor is Money (rule of Money: social praise; segregating power/privilege from least/lost/left-out). Near-nobodies exemplify faithfulness (sinful woman 7:36–50; toll collector 19:1–10; crucified criminal 23:39–43); disciples’ “following” is mostly being “with” Jesus for re-socialization toward Acts witness role.

### C32 — Hostility, devil, ironic fulfillment; holistic salvation
- **Locus:** §2 (end)
- **Quote:** Salvation is neither ethereal nor merely future, but embraces life in the present… The Third Evangelist knows nothing of such dichotomies as those sometimes drawn between social and spiritual or individual and communal
- **Claim:** Green: opponents calculate divine agenda differently and resist Jesus as opposing God; devil opposes divine aim via diabolic oppression and (from Lukan perspective) Jewish leadership; hostility motif builds suspense and shows ironic realization of God’s plan. Salvation restores human life/communities, orders cosmos, commissions practice of grace—embraces social, economic, political totality. God of Israel = Great Benefactor; redemptive purpose in Jesus enables new ways of living.

### C33 — Outline structure of the Gospel (Green’s section plan)
- **Locus:** OUTLINE OF THE GOSPEL OF LUKE
- **Quote:** 1. THE PROLOGUE (1:1–4) … 8. THE EXALTATION OF JESUS (24:1–53)
- **Claim:** Green’s outline (structural map only): 1 Prologue 1:1–4; 2 Birth and childhood 1:5–2:52; 3 Preparation 3:1–4:13; 4 Galilean ministry 4:14–9:50; 5 On the way to Jerusalem 9:51–19:48; 6 Temple teaching 20:1–21:38; 7 Suffering and death 22:1–23:56; 8 Exaltation 24:1–53—with nested subsections as printed in the outline.

### C34 — Ancient first sentences as book jacket / entry to text-world
- **Locus:** §1 THE PROLOGUE (1:1–4) commentary intro
- **Quote:** first sentences are the primary point-of-entry for literary productions… performed much the same purpose as the modern book jacket précis, table of contents, and title page
- **Claim:** Green: rolled scrolls limited browsing; opening put readers/hearers on notice for approach, genre, subject. Beginnings usher from outside-text world into text-world. Quintilian: prefaces prepare well-disposed, attentive, ready-for-instruction audience; literary prefaces follow rhetorical advice. Lucian (*How to Write History*): interest and instruction; narrative trust via claim to “true” version grounded in tradition intimacy, research, and/or personal experience. Openings set network of relations with predecessors.

### C35 — Greek-style preface convention and common ingredients
- **Locus:** Prologue commentary intro
- **Quote:** Luke has inserted at the head of his narrative a Greek-style preface… Prefaces… often shared common ingredients
- **Claim:** Green: Luke follows widespread Greco-Roman preface convention (literary and technical). Common ingredients: (usually) author name; dedication/request; subject importance/implications; (often diminutive) mention of predecessors; methodology claim; transition to work. Luke’s prologue identifies work as “narrative”; first encounter with narrator (outside narrative; later in Acts sometimes as character—“we” passages—not in Gospel). Narratee named Theophilus; narrator unnamed (called Luke). Preface-form indicates release for wider public dissemination.

### C36 — Trustworthiness, narrative voice social location, “one of us”
- **Locus:** Prologue intro, three observations
- **Quote:** Luke is making a claim for the trustworthiness of his book… Luke writes as one of the “people of the Way,” a “Christian”
- **Claim:** Green: (1) Opening designed to impress and underscore believability via rigorous research claim. (2) Voice: written text + vocabulary/style of 1:1–4 suggest narrator of means, educated, probably urban; correlation with scientific tradition suggests social location of technical/professional writing with appreciation for manual labor (vs high-brow disdain for artisans; artisans present in early Christianity); chronological generation not determinable—only that writing follows prior attempts, not that Luke is third-generation or non-observer; claims membership among “us” whose lives shaped by the events. (3) Luke raises “truth”/“certainty”; primary ingredient for Theophilus is *order* of narrative.

### C37 — Narration is proclamation; persuasive order not historical foundation of kerygma
- **Locus:** Prologue intro / purpose
- **Quote:** For him, the narrative is not the basis of proclamation; rather, narration is proclamation
- **Claim:** Green: Luke’s purpose not to provide historical foundation for Christian message; subsequent writers struggle with kerygma/history, but for Luke narration *is* proclamation. Orderly account concerned with persuasion—ordering events for significance so Theophilus (concerned less with Did it happen? than What happened? and What does it mean?) may be encouraged to active faith via more complete accounting of Jesus in significance.

### C38 — Periodic structure and balanced clauses of 1:1–4
- **Locus:** Prologue structure
- **Quote:** Luke 1:1–4 is periodic, with one complete sentence made up of five clauses organized into a balance unity
- **Claim:** Green: one sentence, balanced pairs guide interpretation: many have undertaken // I too decided; set down orderly account // write orderly account; events fulfilled among us // everything; from the beginning // from the very first; handed down to us // so that you may know. Balance of vv 1–2 with vv 3–4 guides prologue interpretation.

### C39 — “Many” predecessors: justification not disparagement; rhetorical “many”
- **Locus:** Prologue v 1 commentary
- **Quote:** Luke mentions other attempts at orderly accounts not to disparage them, but to place his project in their company
- **Claim:** Green: causal first clause justifies rather than primarily motivates writing; Luke identifies with and re-presents previous narratological developments of redemption in Jesus—not mere conservator, not novelist free of tradition. “Many” follows oral/written beginning practice for rhetorical effect, not necessarily a great number; value is vouching for enterprise by association with tradition. Identity of predecessors (whether NT Gospels) unknown to us though assumed known to audience.

### C40 — διήγησις / “orderly account” as narrating God’s mighty deeds
- **Locus:** Prologue v 1 “orderly account”
- **Quote:** For Luke, “narrative” is proclamation… the medium of that proclamation is the narrative account whose “order” is crucial
- **Claim:** Green: rhetorical-tradition and Lucian-historiography readings of “narrative” helpful, but cognate verb “to narrate” characteristically describes God’s mighty deeds (e.g. Acts 9:27 Barnabas narrates Saul’s encounter—third person, persuasive, emphasis on Lord’s doing). Luke uses history to preach persuasive interpretation of God’s work in Jesus and early church.

### C41 — Content: “events… fulfilled among us” as divine affairs across generations
- **Locus:** Prologue v 1b
- **Quote:** “that have been fulfilled among us”… indicate his concern with how the events narrated in the Gospel and Acts are understood as divine affairs
- **Claim:** Green: “events” direct attention to historiographical not biographical interests (even Jesus, Peter, Stephen, Paul sit in larger sequences). “Fulfilled” marks incompleteness-in-themselves needing wider framework—culmination of God’s OT/people purpose; God as unspoken subject; continues through Gospel and Acts. “Among us” + perfect tense + Luke’s self-inclusion = Christian community organic unity across generations, not restricted to first-generation participants.

### C42 — Eyewitnesses and servants of the word as tradition base
- **Locus:** Prologue v 2
- **Quote:** the basis of the tradition of God’s work is not “the many” who had compiled narratives (v 1), but this new group—“eyewitnesses and servants of the word”
- **Claim:** Green: tradition handed “to us” (Luke includes himself with prior narrators); methodology beyond collating existing reports. “Handing on” = technical transmission term, here closer to passing information orally/written to save from oblivion than dogmatic authority (cf. 1 Cor 15:3–5). Appeal to tradition/antiquity shared by historiographical and scientific traditions. Parallel: just as eyewitnesses/ministers passed fulfilled events, compilers shaped coherent narrative unity.

### C43 — “Eyewitness” redefined toward Lukan “witness”
- **Locus:** Prologue v 2
- **Quote:** by “eyewitnesses” he has in mind “witnesses” as that term is developed later—that is, people empowered by the Spirit who “… cannot keep from speaking about what [they] have seen and heard” (Acts 4:20)
- **Claim:** Green: problems—(1) Luke usually prefers “witnesses”; “eyewitness” hapax in Luke-Acts; (2) antiquity “eyewitness” not always personal observation. Historiography’s first step can be site autopsy; Luke uses “eyewitness” in deference to historiographical/scientific traditions but means both less and more—not first step of history-writing or his own firsthand observation. “Seeing” insufficient unless eyes opened (Emmaus 24:13–35). “Eyewitnesses” // “ministers of the word” = same group; “the word” = Christian good news grounded in Jesus’ coming/mission and post-Easter consequences. Contenders from Galilean disciples/resurrection witnesses expand to Barnabas, Paul, others (Acts 1:21–22+).

### C44 — Carefully + orderly; order as persuasive not mere chronology
- **Locus:** Prologue v 3
- **Quote:** “orderly” cannot refer to “adherence to chronological sequence,” nor simply “one after the other.” Rather, Peter’s “ordering” of the account is for the purpose of winning his audience over
- **Claim:** Green: weight on adverbs carefully (ἀκριβῶς) and orderly (καθεξῆς). Carefully usually with investigate, could modify write; claims accuracy; illuminated by Apollos (Acts 18:24–28)—informed yet needing more accurate explication. Orderly = in sequence, but kind of sequence: Lucian on arrangement for beauty/vividness and effect on readers; Acts 11:4 Peter explains “in sequence”—parallel of narrating God’s work; double narration of Cornelius story shows “orderly” = persuasive ordering, not mere chronology—fits Luke’s agenda.

### C45 — Theophilus: real dedicatee of status, not mere symbol; public readership
- **Locus:** Prologue v 3 Theophilus
- **Quote:** such a symbolic rendering is highly unlikely… what we can discern about Theophilus will provide us with some clues about Luke’s purpose, but we should not assume that Theophilus is Luke’s only desired audience or that Theophilus represents Luke’s “community”
- **Claim:** Green: name means “dear to God”/“lover of God” and can point to wider audience, but pure symbol unlikely—(1) common name from 3rd c. B.C.E.; (2) “most excellent” then pointless; (3) symbolic dedication unparalleled in Luke’s literary culture. Which Theophilus unknown; “most excellent” normally for Roman officials, may be honorary—either way advanced status. Theophilus provides inspiration/impetus and recommendation network for wider public audience beyond narratee.

### C46 — Purpose clause: certainty/truth as emphatic persuasion of interpretation
- **Locus:** Prologue v 4
- **Quote:** Luke writes to persuade Theophilus to embrace their certainty… it is the question of interpretation that is vital for him
- **Claim:** Green: final clause defines purpose—Theophilus has some familiarity with fulfilled events but needs instruction to know their truth. “Certainty”/“truth” (ἀσφάλεια) emphatic final word; easy to misread as mere historical-veracity affirmation; terminology suggests convincing nature/certainty of presentation. Message tied to historical origins, so Luke concerned with “what happened,” but vital issue is that events lead to *this* interpretation—the one the narrative will present.

### C47 — How much Theophilus knows: informed but incomplete, Apollos analogy
- **Locus:** Prologue v 4 end
- **Quote:** Theophilus has been informed about the mission of Jesus and the early Christian movement, and that he may even have attached himself to the community of Jesus’ disciples, but key ingredients are lacking in his understanding
- **Claim:** Green: contested options—baptized Christian with formal catechesis vs relative outsider with little more than rumors. Formal apostolic-era catechetical process hard to locate; Luke does not use “inform/instruct” technically. Apollos analogy (Acts 18:24–28): instructed in the Way, knows only John’s baptism; after further explanation shows from Scriptures Messiah is Jesus. By analogy Theophilus informed (possibly attached to community) but lacks key understanding.
